nodes.statement: Assume a Gaussian likelihood and an odd, Lipschitz activation function. Then, for any fixed dataset, as the width tends to infinity, any finite-dimensional distribution of any optimal mean-field variational posterior predictive distribution of a BNN of any depth converges to the corresponding finite-dimensional distribution of the NNGP prior predictive distribution.
assumptions: Assume a Gaussian likelihood and an odd, Lipschitz activation function.
conclusions: Then, for any fixed dataset, as the width tends to infinity, any finite-dimensional distribution of any optimal mean-field variational posterior predictive distribution of a BNN of any depth converges to the corresponding finite-dimensional distribution of the NNGP prior predictive distribution.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:main}
	Assume a Gaussian likelihood and an odd, Lipschitz activation function.
	Then, for any fixed dataset, as the width tends to infinity,
	any finite-dimensional distribution of any optimal mean-field variational posterior predictive distribution of a BNN of any depth converges to the corresponding finite-dimensional distribution of the NNGP prior predictive distribution.

Then, for any fixed dataset, as the width tends to infinity, any finite-dimensional distribution of any optimal mean-field variational posterior predictive distribution of a BNN of any depth converges to the corresponding finite-dimensional distribution of the NNGP prior predictive distribution.
nodes.label: thm:main

\label{prop:existence-mf-solution}
    Let $\mathcal{Q}$ be the family of factorized Gaussian distributions.
    Assume the following:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item The activation $\phi\colon\mathbb{R} \to\mathbb{R}$ is Lipschitz continuous.
        \item The likelihood factorizes over data points: $\log \mathcal{L}(\bm{\uptheta}) = \sum_{n=1}^N \log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))$ for some function $p$.
        \item The likelihood is continuous: for all $\mathbf{y}$, the function $\mathbf{f} \mapsto p(\mathbf{y} \,|\, \mathbf{f})$ is continuous.
        \item The likelihood is upper bounded: there exists a $C \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{f}$, $\log p(\mathbf{y} \,|\, \mathbf{f}) \leq C$.
        \item The likelihood admits a quadratic lower bound:
        for all $\mathbf{y}$, the function $\mathbf{f} \mapsto \log p(\mathbf{y} \,|\, \mathbf{f})$ can be lower bounded by a quadratic function in $\mathbf{f}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then $arg\,max_{Q \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(Q)$ is non-empty:
    an optimal mean-field solution $Q \in arg\,max_{Q \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(Q)$ exists.

nodes.raw_latex:
Let $I$ denote the total number of parameters in the network.
Then the variational optimization problem can be phrased as 

\begin{align}
    \relax_{\ensuremath{Q} \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q}) \quad \text{where}
    \quad \operatorname{ELBO} \colon \mathcal{Q} \to \mathbb{R},
    \quad \mathcal{Q} = \set{
        \mathcal{N}(\bm{\upmu}, \operatorname{diag}(\bm{\upsigma}^2)) : \bm{\upmu} \in \mathbb{R}^I, \, \bm{\upsigma}^2 \in (0, \infty)^I
    }.
\end{align}
Call a sequence $(\mathcal{N}(\bm{\upmu}_k, \operatorname{diag}(\bm{\upsigma}_k^2)))_{k \ge 1} \subseteq \mathcal{Q}$ \emph{parameter convergent} [to $\mathcal{N}(\bm{\upmu}, \operatorname{diag}(\bm{\upsigma}^2)) \in \mathcal{Q}$] if $(\bm{\upmu}_k, \bm{\upsigma}_i^2)_{k \ge 1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I \times (0, \infty)^I$ is convergent [to $(\bm{\upmu}, \bm{\upsigma}) \in \mathbb{R}^I \times (0, \infty)^I$].
Using the definition of the supremum, extract a sequence $(Q_k)_{k \ge 1} \subseteq \mathcal{Q}$ such that $\operatorname{ELBO}(Q_k) \to \relax_{\ensuremath{Q} \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q})$.
The argument now consists of two parts.
First, we show that there exists a subsequence $(Q_{n_k})_{k \ge 1} \subseteq (Q_k)_{k \ge 1}$ which is parameter convergent to some limit $Q^* \in \mathcal{Q}$ (compactness).
Second, we show that $\operatorname{ELBO}$ is upper semi-continuous with respect to parameter convergence (continuity).
Assuming the two parts,
\begin{align}
    \relax_{\ensuremath{Q} \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q})
    = \lim_{k \to \infty} \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q}_k)
    = \relax_{k \to \infty}\, \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q}_{n_k})
    \overset{\text{(i)}}{\le}  \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q}^*),
\end{align}
where we use in (i) that $\operatorname{ELBO}$ is upper semi-continuous with respect to parameter convergence. 
Therefore, $\ensuremath{Q}^* \in arg\,max_{Q \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(Q)$, which concludes the proof.

\paragraph{Compactness.}
We show that there exists a subsequence $(Q_{n_k})_{k \ge 1} \subseteq (Q_k)_{k \ge 1}$ which is parameter convergent to some limit $Q^* \in \mathcal{Q}$.
Let $P = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) \in \mathcal{Q}$ be the prior.
Assume that $\operatorname{ELBO}(P) < \relax_{\ensuremath{Q} \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q})$; for if equality holds, an optimal mean-field solution certainly exists.
Since $\operatorname{ELBO}(Q_k) \to \relax_{\ensuremath{Q} \in \mathcal{Q}} \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q})$, it follows that, for large enough $k$, $\operatorname{ELBO}(P) < \operatorname{ELBO}(\ensuremath{Q}_k)$.
Therefore, by step 2 from \cref{sec:proof-sketch}, it follows that there exists a $C > 0$ such that, for large enough $k$, $\operatorname{KL}(Q_k, P) < C$.
Consequently, denoting $Q_k = \mathcal{N}(\bm{\upmu}_k, \bm{\upsigma}^2_k)$, by \cref{app:parameter-bounds} and the observation that $r(a) < c$ for $c \ge 0$ implies that $a \in [R^{-1}, R]$ for some $R \in [1, \infty)$, it follows that there exists an $R \in [1, \infty)$ such that, for large enough $k$ and all $i \in [I]$, $\abs{\mu_{k,i}} \le R$ and $R^{-1} \le \abs{\sigma^2_{k,i}} \le R$.
Hence, by Bolzano--Weierstrass, there exists a subsequence $(Q_{n_k})_{k \ge 1} \subseteq (Q_k)_{k \ge 1}$ which is parameter convergent to some limit $Q^* \in \mathcal{Q}$.











\paragraph{Continuity.}
Let $(Q_k)_{k \ge 1} \subseteq \mathcal{Q}$ be parameter convergent to some $Q \in \mathcal{Q}$.
To conclude the proof, we show that
$
    \relax_{k \to \infty}\, \operatorname{ELBO}(Q_k) \le \operatorname{ELBO}(Q).
$
Decompose the ELBO as follows:
\begin{equation} \textstyle
    \operatorname{ELBO}(Q_k)
    = \sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{Q_k}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))] - \operatorname{KL}(Q_k, P).
\end{equation}
From \cref{app:parameter-bounds}, $Q \mapsto {-\operatorname{KL}}(Q, P)$ is clearly continuous with respect to parameter convergence, so it is also upper semi-continuous with respect to parameter convergence.
Hence, it remains to show that
\begin{equation}
    \relax_{k \to \infty}\,\mathbb{E}_{Q_k}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))]
    \le \mathbb{E}_{Q}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))].
\end{equation}
To show this, we use the reparametrization trick:
rewrite $\mathbb{E}_{Q_k}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))] = \mathbb{E}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}_n))]$ where
\begin{align}
    \mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}) &= \tfrac1{\sqrt{D\ss{o}}}(\mathbf{S}^{Q_k}_{L+1} \circ \mathbfcal{E}_{L+1} + \mathbf{M}^{Q_k}_{L+1}) \phi(\mathbf{z}^{Q_k}_{L}) + (\mathbf{s}^{Q_k}_{L+1} \circ \bm{\upvarepsilon}_{L+1} + \mathbf{m}^{Q_k}_{L+1}), \\
    \mathbf{z}^{Q_k}_\ell
    &= \tfrac1{\sqrt{M}}(\mathbf{S}^{Q_k}_\ell \circ \mathbfcal{E}_\ell + \mathbf{M}^{Q_k}_\ell) \phi(\mathbf{z}^{Q_k}_{\ell-1}) + (\mathbf{s}^{Q_k}_\ell \circ \bm{\upvarepsilon}_\ell + \mathbf{m}^{Q_k}_\ell),
    \qquad\qquad \ell = L, \ldots, 2, \\
    \mathbf{z}^{Q_k}_1
    &= \tfrac1{\sqrt{D\ss{i}}}(\mathbf{S}^{Q_k}_1 \circ \mathbfcal{E}_1 + \mathbf{M}^{Q_k}_1) \mathbf{x} + (\mathbf{s}^{Q_k}_1 \circ \bm{\upvarepsilon}_1 + \mathbf{m}^{Q_k}_1).
\end{align}
where $(\mathbfcal{E}_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L+1}$ are matrices of i.i.d.~standard Gaussian random variables, $(\bm{\upvarepsilon}_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L+1}$ are vectors of i.i.d.~standard Gaussian random variables,
$(\mathbf{M}^{Q_k}_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L+1}$ are matrices consisting of the means of each weight in each layer under $\ensuremath{Q}_k$,
$(\mathbf{m}^{Q_k}_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L+1}$ are vectors consisting of the means of each bias in each layer under $\ensuremath{Q}_k$, 
$(\mathbf{S}^{Q_k}_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L+1}$ are matrices consisting of the standard deviations of each weight in each layer under $\ensuremath{Q}_k$, and
$(\mathbf{s}^{Q_k}_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L+1}$ are vectors consisting of the standard deviations of each bias in each layer under $\ensuremath{Q}_k$.
Since $\phi$ is Lipschitz, it is continuous, so clearly $\mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}) \to \mathbf{f}^{Q}(\mathbf{x})$.
Let $C$ be the upper bound on the likelihood.
Then
\begin{align*}
    \relax_{k \to \infty}\,\mathbb{E}_{Q_k}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))]
    &= C + \relax_{k \to \infty}\,\mathbb{E}[-C + \log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))] \\
    &= C - \relax_{k \to \infty}\,\mathbb{E}[C - \log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}_n))] \\
    &\overset{\smash{\text{(i)}}}{\le} C - \mathbb{E}[\relax_{k \to \infty}\,(C - \log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}_n)))] \\
    &\overset{\smash{\text{(ii)}}}{=} \vphantom{\relax_{k \to \infty}} C - \mathbb{E}[C - \log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}^{Q}(\mathbf{x}_n))] \\
    &=\vphantom{\relax_{k \to \infty}} \mathbb{E}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}^{Q}(\mathbf{x}_n))] \\
    &= \mathbb{E}_{Q}[\log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_n))],
\end{align*}
where in (i) we use Fatou's lemma in combination with that $C - \log p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}_n)) \ge 0$ by definition of $C$ and in (ii) we use (ii.a) continuity of $\mathbf{f} \mapsto p(\mathbf{y}_n \,|\, \mathbf{f})$ and (ii.b) $\mathbf{f}^{Q_k}(\mathbf{x}_n) \to \mathbf{f}^{Q}(\mathbf{x}_n)$.

We prove each bound in turn.
\paragraph{(i):}
    This follows directly from \cref{lem:gaussian-kl} and non-negativity of norms.
    
\paragraph{(ii):}
    To prove (ii), we recall the identity $\log (a') \leq a'-1$ for all $a'>0.$ Define $a'=\sqrt{a}$. Then $\log(a) = 2(\sqrt{a} - 1)$. 
    
    
    





Rearranging, $\log(a) \le 2 \sqrt{a} - 2$ for all $a > 0$. Then compute
    \begin{equation}
        r(a) = a - 1 - \log(a)
        \ge a - 1 - (2 \sqrt{a} - 2)
        =  a - 2 \sqrt{a} + 1
        = (\sqrt{a} - 1)^2.
    \end{equation}
    
\paragraph{(iii):}    
    For (iii), estimate
    \begin{equation}
        \sigma\ss{max} - 1
        \le \abs{\sigma\ss{max} - 1}
        \le \norm{\bm{\upsigma}_{\ensuremath{Q}} - \mathbf{1}}_2
        \le \sqrt{2 \operatorname{KL}(\ensuremath{Q}, \ensuremath{P})},
    \end{equation}
where the last inequality uses (ii).

\paragraph{(iv):}     
    For (iv), factoring the difference of two squares, 
	
	
	\begin{align}
		\norm{\bm{\upsigma}_{\ensuremath{Q}}^2 - \mathbf{1}}_2^2
		&\textstyle= \sum_{i=1}^I (\sigma^2_i -1)^2 
		\\
		&\textstyle =  \sum_{i=1}^I (\sigma_i +1)^2 (\sigma_i -1)^2 \\
 		&\textstyle\le \sum_{i=1}^I (\sigma\ss{max} + 1)^2 (\sigma_i-1)^2
		\\
		&\textstyle= (\sigma\ss{max} + 1)^2 \sum_{i=1}^I (\sigma_i-1)^2
		\\
		&\textstyle= (\sigma\ss{max} + 1)^2 \norm{\bm{\upsigma}_{\ensuremath{Q}} - \mathbf{1}}_2^2
		\\
		&\le (2 + \sqrt{2 \operatorname{KL}(\ensuremath{Q}, \ensuremath{P})})^2 (2 \operatorname{KL}(\ensuremath{Q}, \ensuremath{P}))
	\end{align}
where in the final inequality we have used (ii) and (iii).

nodes.statement: We slightly generalise Exercise 5.14 from citetWainwright:2019:High-Dimensional_Statistics_A_Non-Asymptotic_Viewpoint. To begin with, rewrite the operator norm as normA_2 = relax_(u, v) in S^I - 1 times S^J - 1 lrau, A v. Define the zero-mean Gaussian process Z_u, v = lrau, A v indexed on S^I - 1 times S^J - 1 and define S by S_i,j = V[A_i,j] le sigma^2. Note that, by independence of the entries of A, E[(Z_u,v - Z_w, x)^2] &= E[Z^2_u, v - 2 Z_u,v Z_w, x + Z^2_w, x] \\ &= textstyle sum_i=1,j=1^I,J S_ij u_i^2 v_j^2 - 2 sum_i=1,j=1^I,J S_ij u_i v_j w_i x_j + sum_i=1,j=1^I,J S_ij w_i^2 x_j^2 \\ &= textstyle sum_i=1,j=1^I,J S_ij (u_i v_j - w_i x_j)^2 \\ &le textstyle sigma^2 sum_i=1,j=1^I,J (u_i v_j - w_i x_j)^2 \\ &= sigma^2 normu v^T - w x^TssF^2. Also consider the zero-mean Gaussian process Y_u, v = sigma lrau, bmupvarepsilon_1 + sigma lrav, bmupvarepsilon_2 again indexed on S^I - 1 times S^J - 1, where bmupvarepsilon_1 in R^I and bmupvarepsilon_2 in R^J are standard Gaussian vectors. Then E[(Y_u, v - Y_w, x)^2] &= sigma^2 E[(lrau - w, bmupvarepsilon_1 + lrav - x, bmupvarepsilon_2)^2] \\ &= sigma^2 E[lrau - w, bmupvarepsilon_1^2 + lrav - x, bmupvarepsilon_2^2] \\ &= sigma^2 (normu - w_2^2 + normv - x_2^2). Using that normu_2 = normv_2 =normx_2 =normw_2 = 1, careful algebra citep[see, e.g., page 164 from][]Wainwright:2019:High-Dimensional_Statistics_A_Non-Asymptotic_Viewpoint shows that normu v^T - w x^TssF^2 le normu - w_2^2 + normv - x_2^2: (u_i v_j - w_i x_j)^2 &= (u_i v_j - w_i v_j + w_i v_j - w_i x_j)^2 \\ &= (u_i - w_i)^2 v_j^2 + w_i^2 (v_j - x_j)^2 + 2 (u_i v_j - w_i v_j) (w_i v_j - w_i x_j) \\ &= (u_i - w_i)^2 v_j^2 + w_i^2 (v_j - x_j)^2 + 2 (u_i w_i - w_i^2) (v^2_j - v_j x_j). Therefore, summing over i in [I] and j in [J] and using that normv_2 = normw_2 = 1, normu v^T - w x^T^2ssF = normu - w_2^2 + normv - x_2^2 + 2(lrau, w - 1)(1 - lrav, x) le normu - w_2^2 + normv - x_2^2 where the inequality follows from additionally using that normu_2 = normx_2 = 1. Using this result, we find E[(Z_u,v - Z_w, x)^2] le E[(Y_u, v - Y_w, x)^2]. Hence, denoting Z^* = relax_(u, v) in S^I - 1 times S^J - 1 Z_u,v and Y^* = relax_(u, v) in S^I - 1 times S^J - 1 Y_u,v, by the Sudakov--Fernique comparison theorem citep[Theorem 5.27,][]Wainwright:2019:High-Dimensional_Statistics_A_Non-Asymptotic_Viewpoint, we conclude that E[normA_2] = E[Z^*] le E[Y^*] oversetsmash(i)= sigma\,E[normbmupvarepsilon_1_2 + normbmupvarepsilon_2_2] oversetsmash(ii)le sigma(sqrtI + sqrtJ) where (i) follows from that the suprema are achieved by bmupvarepsilon_1/normbmupvarepsilon_1_2 and bmupvarepsilon_2/normbmupvarepsilon_2_2 for u and v, respectively, and (ii) follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the square root. For the second statement, assume that all entries of A have variance one, so sigma^2=1. We apply concentration of Gaussian suprema citep[e.g., Exercise 5.10 by][]Wainwright:2019:High-Dimensional_Statistics_A_Non-Asymptotic_Viewpoint to Z_u,v: P( abs Z^* - E[Z^*] ge delta ) le 2 exp(-tfrac12 v delta^2) where v = relax_(u, v) in S^I - 1 times S^J - 1 V[Z_u,v] = relax_(u, v) in S^I - 1 times S^J - 1normu_2^2 normv_2^2 = 1. Therefore, using the bound on E[Z^*] from the first statement, P(normA_2 ge 2 sqrtI lor J + delta) le 2 exp(-tfrac12 delta^2), which concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Convergence of second moment prediction
nodes.statement: Let Q be a mean-field variational posterior and P=N(0,I) denote the prior over a neural network with L hidden layers and M neurons per hidden layer. Suppose phisse=alpha for some alpha in R and phicolon R to R is 1-Lipschitz. Let x in R^Dssi and let widetildef_theta(x) = f_theta(x) - tfracalphasqrtMW_L+11 - b_L+1 denote the network output excluding final bias and even part of the final activation. Then normE_Q[tildef_bmuptheta^2(x)] - E_P[tildef_bmuptheta^2(x)]_infty le c_1L^1/2 rho_alpha, M^L frac alpha^2 + 1 + tfrac1Dssinormx_2^2 sqrtM sqrtKL(ensuremathQ, ensuremathP) (2KL(ensuremathQ, ensuremathP) lor 1)^L+tfrac12, where c_1 = 16 + 25sqrt2 in (51, 52) and where rho_alpha, M in (17, 97) is defined in creflem:diag-frob-norm.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{thm:app-convergence-of-variance}
nodes.statement: We will repeatedly use cyclic property and linearity of trace. Hence, we briefly recall that for conformable matrix A, B, we have tr(AB)=tr(BA) and E[tr(AB)] = tr(E[AB]). We also observe that the trace of a 1times 1 matrix is simply the corresponding scalar. It suffices to consider an arbitrary output component. Let widetildef(x) = widetildef(x)_i denote an arbitrary output component i and let w_L+1 denote row i of W_L+1, so that widetildef(x) = tfrac1M w_L+1^Tphisso(z_L). Mwidetildef(x)^2 &= w_L+1^Tphisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T w_L+1 \\ & =trleft(w_L+1^Tphisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T w_L+1right) \\ & = trleft(w_L+1w_L+1^Tphisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T right). Recall Sigma_Q =E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1w_L+1^T] - E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]^T, which is a diagonal matrix (by indpendence) with the variances of w_L+1 as entries. Then, adding and subtracting E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]^T, and using that w_L+1 is independent of z_L by the independence assumption E_ensuremathQ[widetildef(x)^2] &= tfrac1Mtr((E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]^T + Sigma_Q) E_ensuremathQ[phisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T] ) \\ & = tfrac1Mtr(E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]^TE_ensuremathQ[phisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T] ) + tfrac1Mtr(Sigma_QE_ensuremathQ[phisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T]) \\ & = tfrac1ME_ensuremathQ[w_L+1]^TE_ensuremathQ[phisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T]E_ensuremathQ[w_L+1] + D^i_ensuremathQ \\ &= O^i_ensuremathQ(x) + D^i_ensuremathQ(x). Also, E_ensuremathP[widetildef(x)^2] =D^i_ensuremathP(x) since E_ensuremathP[w_L+1]=0. So, |E_ensuremathQ[widetildef(x)^2] - E_ensuremathP[widetildef(x)^2]| &= |O^i_ensuremathQ(x) + D^i_ensuremathQ(x) - D^i_ensuremathP(x)| \\ & leq |O^i_ensuremathQ(x)| + |D^i_ensuremathQ(x) - D^i_ensuremathP(x)|. The final result is obtained by plugging in the expressions from Lemmas and , noting that gamma_alpha le gamma_alpha, M.
nodes.raw_latex:
We will repeatedly use cyclic property and linearity of trace. Hence, we briefly recall that for conformable matrix $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}$, we have $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})$ and $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})] = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}])$. We also observe that the trace of a $1\times 1$ matrix is simply the corresponding scalar.

It suffices to consider an arbitrary output component. Let $\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \widetilde{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x})_i$ denote an arbitrary output component $i$ and let $\mathbf{w}_{L+1}$ denote row $i$ of $\mathbf{W}_{L+1}$, so that $\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac{1}{M} \mathbf{w}_{L+1}^T\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_L)$. 
\begin{align}
M\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x})^2 &= \mathbf{w}_{L+1}^{\text{\textsf{T}}}\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}} \mathbf{w}_{L+1} \\
& =\operatorname{tr}\left(\mathbf{w}_{L+1}^{\text{\textsf{T}}}\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}} \mathbf{w}_{L+1}\right) \\
& = \operatorname{tr}\left(\mathbf{w}_{L+1}\mathbf{w}_{L+1}^{\text{\textsf{T}}}\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}} \right).
\end{align}
Recall $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{Q} =\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}\mathbf{w}_{L+1}^{\text{\textsf{T}}}] -  \mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]^{\text{\textsf{T}}}$, which is a diagonal matrix (by indpendence) with the variances of $\mathbf{w}_{L+1}$ as entries. Then, adding and subtracting $\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]^{\text{\textsf{T}}}$, and using that $\mathbf{w}_{L+1}$ is independent of $\mathbf{z}_{L}$ by the independence assumption
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x})^2] &=
    \tfrac{1}{M}\operatorname{tr}((\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]^{\text{\textsf{T}}} + \mathbf{\Sigma}_{Q}) \mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}] ) \\
    & = \tfrac{1}{M}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]^{\text{\textsf{T}}}\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}] ) + \tfrac{1}{M}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{Q}\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}]) \\
    & = \tfrac{1}{M}\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]^{\text{\textsf{T}}}\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})\phi\ss{o}(\mathbf{z}_{L})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}]\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}] + D^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}} \\
    &= O^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}}(\mathbf{x}) + D^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}}(\mathbf{x}).
\end{align}
Also, $\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{P}}[\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x})^2] =D^{i}_{\ensuremath{P}}(\mathbf{x})$ since $\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{P}}[\mathbf{w}_{L+1}]=0$. So,
\begin{align}
    |\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}}[\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x})^2] - \mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{P}}[\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x})^2]| &= |O^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}}(\mathbf{x}) + D^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}}(\mathbf{x}) - D^{i}_{\ensuremath{P}}(\mathbf{x})| \\
    & \leq |O^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}}(\mathbf{x})|  + |D^{i}_{\ensuremath{Q}}(\mathbf{x}) - D^{i}_{\ensuremath{P}}(\mathbf{x})|.
\end{align}
The final result is obtained by plugging in the expressions from Lemmas \ref{lem:app-diagonal-variance} and \ref{lem:app-off-diagonal-variance}, noting that $\gamma_{\alpha} \le \gamma_{\alpha, M}$.

To integrate the tail bound, use the layer cake trick: E[normA^2_2] &= int_0^infty ensuremathP(normA^2_2 > u) isd u \\ &le 4(I lor J) + int_0^infty ensuremathP(normA^2_2 > 4(I lor J) + u) isd u. Consider the change of variables defined by 4(I lor J) + u = (2 sqrtI lor J + v)^2. Then sd u = 2( 2sqrtI lor J + v) isd v, so E[normA^2_2] &le 4(I lor J) + 2int_0^infty ensuremathP(normA_2 > 2 sqrtI lor J + v) (2 sqrtI lor J + v) isd v \\ &levphantomint_0^infty 4(I lor J) + 4int_0^infty e^-tfrac12 v^2 (2 sqrtI lor J + v) isd v \\ &=vphantomint_0^infty 4(I lor J) + 4 sqrt2pi sqrtI lor J + 4. The claimed bound then follows by checking cases.

Hence, by the triangle inequality, normE[z_1^2]_infty &le tfrac2M_2 relax_m \abslraVssd[w_m], E[phi_2^2(z_2)] \ + relax_m \absC + tfrac2M_2 lraE^2[w_m], E[phi_2^2(z_2)]\ + 2\, normE[b^2]_infty. Consider the middle term in crefeqn:z1_infty. We have C + tfrac2M_2 lraE^2[w_m], E[phi_2^2(z_2)] &= tfrac2M_2 lraE[w_m], E[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T] E[w_m] \\ &le tfrac2M_2 normE[w_m]_2^2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2, where the second inequality follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the definition of the operator norm. Therefore, relax_m \ absC + tfrac2M_2 lraE^2[w_m], E[phi_2^2(z_2)] \ &le tfrac2M_2 relax_m \ normE[w_m]_2^2 \ normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2 \\ &le tfrac2M_2 normE[W]ssF^2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2. The result follows by applying creflem:parameter_bound and crefprop:optimised_param_bound. Similarly, using normE[z_2^2]_1 le M_2 normE[z_2^2]_infty, we can again plug into crefeqn:z1_infty to obtain normE[z_1^2]_infty &le 2 normVssd[vec(W)]_infty normE[z_2^2]_infty + tfrac2M_2 normE[W]ssF^2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2 + 2 normE[b^2]_infty \\ &le 2( normVssd[vec(W)]_infty + normE[b^2]_infty ) (1 lor normE[z_2^2]_infty) + tfrac2M_2 normE[W]ssF^2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2.

To begin with, note that (tfracalphasqrtM_2 W 1 + b)^2 &= (tfracalphasqrtM_2 (W - E[W]) 1 + tfracalphasqrtM_2 E[W] 1 + b)^2 \\ &preceq 3tfracalpha^2M_2 ((W - E[W]) 1)^2 + 3tfracalpha^2M_2 (E[W] 1)^2 + 3 b^2 \\ &preceq 3tfracalpha^2M_2 ((W - E[W]) 1)^2 + 3tfracalpha^2M_2 normE[W]_infty^2 norm1_infty^2 1 + 3 b^2 \\ &oversetsmash(i)preceq 3tfracalpha^2M_2 ((W - E[W]) 1)^2 + 3alpha^2 normE[W]ssF^2 1 + 3 b^2 where the squares and inequalities are element-wise and in (i) we use that normE[W]_infty le sqrtM_2 normE[W]ssF. For the first term, consider the mtextsuperscriptth element and use independence of the elements of W: E[tfrac1M_2((W - E[W]) 1)^2]_m &= textstyle tfrac1M_2 Ebig[ big(sum_m'=1^M_2(W_m,m' - E[W_m,m'])big)^2 big] \\ &= textstyle tfrac1M_2 sum_m'=1^M_2 E[(W_m,m' - E[W_m,m'])^2] \\ &le normVssd[vec(W)]_infty. \label{rem:inf_offset}
    Like in \cref{rem:outer_offset}, apply \cref{lem:inf} to the triple $(\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{z}_2, \tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{b})$ where $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, not $\mathbf{z}_2$, are element-wise independent and symmetric around their means.
    To write down the result, we need to estimate $\norm{\mathbb{E}[(\tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{b})^2]}_\infty$.
    To begin with, note that
    \begin{align}
        (\tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{b})^2
        &= (\tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} (\mathbf{W} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]) \mathbf{1} + \tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}] \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{b})^2 \\
        &\preceq 3\tfrac{\alpha^2}{M_2} ((\mathbf{W} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]) \mathbf{1})^2 + 3\tfrac{\alpha^2}{M_2} (\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}] \mathbf{1})^2 + 3 \mathbf{b}^2 \\
        &\preceq 3\tfrac{\alpha^2}{M_2} ((\mathbf{W} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]) \mathbf{1})^2 + 3\tfrac{\alpha^2}{M_2} \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}_\infty^2 \norm{\mathbf{1}}_\infty^2 \mathbf{1} + 3 \mathbf{b}^2 \\
        &\overset{\smash{\text{(i)}}}{\preceq} 3\tfrac{\alpha^2}{M_2} ((\mathbf{W} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]) \mathbf{1})^2 + 3\alpha^2 \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}\ss{F}^2 \mathbf{1} + 3 \mathbf{b}^2
    \end{align}
    where the squares and inequalities are element-wise and in (i) we use that $\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}_\infty \le \sqrt{M_2} \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}\ss{F}$.
    For the first term, consider the $m$\textsuperscript{th} element and use independence of the elements of $\mathbf{W}$:
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}[\tfrac{1}{M_2}((\mathbf{W} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]) \mathbf{1})^2]_m
        &= \textstyle
            \tfrac{1}{M_2} \mathbb{E}\big[
                \big(\sum_{m'=1}^{M_2}(W_{m,m'} - \mathbb{E}[W_{m,m'}])\big)^2
            \big] \\
        &= \textstyle
            \tfrac{1}{M_2}
                \sum_{m'=1}^{M_2} \mathbb{E}[(W_{m,m'} - \mathbb{E}[W_{m,m'}])^2] \\
        &\le \norm{\mathbb{V}\ss{d}[\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{W})]}_{\infty}.
    \end{align}
    Therefore, 
    \begin{equation}
        \norm{\mathbb{E}[(\tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{b})^2]}_\infty
        \le 3 \alpha^2 \norm{\mathbb{V}\ss{d}[\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{W})]}_{\infty} + 3 \alpha^2 \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}\ss{F}^2 + 3 \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{b}^2]}_\infty,
    \end{equation}
    so, by \cref{lem:outer} (specifically \cref{eqn:lem-outer-part1}),
    \begin{align}
        &\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_{1}^2]}_\infty \nonumber \\
        &\quad\le
            2 \norm{\mathbb{V}\ss{d}[\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{W})]}_\infty 
            \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_2^2]}_\infty 
            + \tfrac2{M_2} \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}\ss{F}^2 
            \norm{\mathbb{E}[\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}]}_2
            + 2\norm{\mathbb{E}[(\tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt{M_2}} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{b})^2]}_\infty, \\
        &\quad\le
            2 \norm{\mathbb{V}\ss{d}[\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{W})]}_\infty 
            (3 \alpha^2 + \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_2^2]}_\infty) 
            + 2\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}]}\ss{F}^2 
            (3\alpha^2 + \tfrac1{M_2} \norm{\mathbb{E}[\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}]}_2)
            + 6 \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{b}^2]}_\infty \\
        &\quad\le
            6 (\sqrt{2} + K)^2(\alpha^2 + 1\lor \norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_2^2]}_\infty)
            + 6K^2 
            (\alpha^2 + \tfrac1{M_2} \norm{\mathbb{E}[\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}]}_2).
    \end{align}
    Similarly, by \cref{eqn:lem-outer-part2}, we can write this inequality in terms of $\tfrac1{M_2}\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_2^2]}_1$ instead of $\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_2^2]}_\infty$:
    \begin{align}
        &\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_{1}^2]}_\infty
            \le
            6 (\sqrt{2} + K)^2(\alpha^2 + 1\lor \tfrac1{M_2}\norm{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_2^2]}_1)
            + 6K^2 
            (\alpha^2 + \tfrac1{M_2} \norm{\mathbb{E}[\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})\phi_2(\mathbf{z}_{2})^{\text{\textsf{T}}}]}_2).
    \end{align}

To begin with, note that (tfracalphasqrtM_2 W 1 + b)^2 &= (tfracalphasqrtM_2 (W - E[W]) 1 + tfracalphasqrtM_2 E[W] 1 + b)^2 \\ &preceq 3tfracalpha^2M_2 ((W - E[W]) 1)^2 + 3tfracalpha^2M_2 (E[W] 1)^2 + 3 b^2 \\ &preceq 3tfracalpha^2M_2 ((W - E[W]) 1)^2 + 3tfracalpha^2M_2 normE[W]_infty^2 norm1_infty^2 1 + 3 b^2 \\ &oversetsmash(i)preceq 3tfracalpha^2M_2 ((W - E[W]) 1)^2 + 3alpha^2 normE[W]ssF^2 1 + 3 b^2 where the squares and inequalities are element-wise and in (i) we use that normE[W]_infty le sqrtM_2 normE[W]ssF. For the first term, consider the mtextsuperscriptth element and use independence of the elements of W: E[tfrac1M_2((W - E[W]) 1)^2]_m &= textstyle tfrac1M_2 Ebig[ big(sum_m'=1^M_2(W_m,m' - E[W_m,m'])big)^2 big] \\ &= textstyle tfrac1M_2 sum_m'=1^M_2 E[(W_m,m' - E[W_m,m'])^2] \\ &le normVssd[vec(W)]_infty. Therefore, normE[(tfracalphasqrtM_2 W 1 + b)^2]_infty le 3 alpha^2 normVssd[vec(W)]_infty + 3 alpha^2 normE[W]ssF^2 + 3 normE[b^2]_infty, so, by creflem:outer (specifically crefeqn:lem-outer-part1), &normE[z_1^2]_infty nonumber \\ & le 2 normVssd[vec(W)]_infty normE[z_2^2]_infty + tfrac2M_2 normE[W]ssF^2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2 + 2normE[(tfracalphasqrtM_2 W 1 + b)^2]_infty, \\ & le 2 normVssd[vec(W)]_infty (3 alpha^2 + normE[z_2^2]_infty) + 2normE[W]ssF^2 (3alpha^2 + tfrac1M_2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2) + 6 normE[b^2]_infty \\ & le 6 (sqrt2 + K)^2(alpha^2 + 1lor normE[z_2^2]_infty) + 6K^2 (alpha^2 + tfrac1M_2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2). Similarly, by crefeqn:lem-outer-part2, we can write this inequality in terms of tfrac1M_2normE[z_2^2]_1 instead of normE[z_2^2]_infty: &normE[z_1^2]_infty le 6 (sqrt2 + K)^2(alpha^2 + 1lor tfrac1M_2normE[z_2^2]_1) + 6K^2 (alpha^2 + tfrac1M_2 normE[phi_2(z_2)phi_2(z_2)^T]_2).

nodes.name: Proof of case $\alpha = 0$
nodes.statement: For notational convenience, define a_ell = 1 lor normE[z_ell^2]_infty and b_ell = normE[phi(z_ell)phi(z_ell)^T]_2. Also take a_0 = 1lor \|x\|^2_2. Apply creflem:inf with phi_2 given by the identity function and z_2 = x. Then a_1 &leq 2left((sqrt2+K)^2 (1 lor tfrac1Dssinormx^2_1) + tfrac1Dssi K^2 normxx^T_2 right) \\ &le 2left(8(1 lor K)^2 (1 lor tfrac1Dssinormx_2^2) + tfrac1Dssi K^2 \|x\|_2^2 right) \\ & leq 18(1 lor K^2)(1 lor tfrac1Dssinormx^2_2) where the second inequality follows from sqrt2 + K le sqrt2(1 + K) le 2sqrt2(1 lor K) and normxx^T_2 = normx_2^2. By creflem:inf we have a_ell leq 2left((sqrt2+K)^2 a_ell-1 + tfrac1M K^2 b_ell-1 right). Further, by creflem:outer, we have b_ell-1 leq 4sqrtM(a_ell-1 + K^2\, a_ell-2) . Combining these estimates yields a_ell &leq 2left((sqrt2+K)^2 a_ell-1 + tfrac4sqrtM K^2 left(a_ell-1 + K^2 a_ell-2right. right) \\ & leq 2left(8(1lor K^2) a_ell-1 + tfrac4sqrtM K^2 left(a_ell-1 + K^2 a_ell-2right) right) \\ & le (16+tfrac8sqrtM) (1 lor K^2) a_ell-1 + tfrac8sqrtM (1 lor K^4) a_ell-2. Assuming M ge 36, we further simplify a_ell &leq (16+tfrac43) (1 lor K^2) a_ell-1 + tfrac43 (1 lor K^4) a_ell-2. We choose M ge 36 for convenience when subsequently applying this lemma. We will return to the general case of M ge 1 later. First, notice crefeqn:second_order_recursion is a homogeneous second-order linear recurrence relation. By finding the roots of the characteristic polynomial associated to this recurrence relation, a_ell leq c_0Big(gamma (1 lor K^2)Big)^ell for some c_0 and gamma = tfrac23(13+2sqrt43 in (17,18), which can be proved by induction. Checking initial conditions, we see that we can take c_0 = 1lor \|x\|^2 , yielding the bound a_ell &leq Big(gamma(1 lor K^2)Big)^ell (1lor tfrac1Dssi \|x\|^2_2). On the other hand, if 1 le M < 36, by the same reasoning the bound holds with constant gamma = 2(6+sqrt38) in (24,25).

nodes.name: Proof of case $\alpha \neq 0$
nodes.statement: The proof for the case alpha neq 0 proceeds like the case alpha = 0, but uses crefrem:outer_offset,rem:inf_offset instead of creflem:outer,lem:inf. Analogously define a_ell = alpha^2 + 1 lor normE[z_ell^2]_infty, a_0 = alpha^2 + 1 lor normx^2_2, and b_ell = normE[phi(z_ell)phi(z_ell)^T]_2. To begin with, apply crefrem:inf_offset with phi_2 given by the identity function and z_2 = x: a_1 &le alpha^2 + 6(sqrt2 + K)^2(alpha^2 + 1 lor tfrac1Dssinormx^2_1)+ 6K^2(alpha^2 + tfrac1Dssi normx x^T_2) \\ &le 48(1 lor K^2)(alpha^2 + 1 lor tfrac1Dssinormx_2^2)+ 7K^2(alpha^2 + normx^2_2) \\ &le 55(1 lor K^2)(alpha^2 + 1 lor tfrac1Dssinormx^2_2). For 1 < ell le L, a_ell &le alpha^2 + 48(1 lor K^2)a_ell - 1 + 6K^2(alpha^2 + tfrac1Mb_ell-1). By crefrem:outer_offset, b_ell - 1 le 8 sqrtM (normE[z_ell-1^2]_infty + K^2 a_ell - 2). Plugging the expression for b_ell-1 into the expression for a_ell, a_ell &le alpha^2 + 48(1 lor K^2)a_ell - 1 + 6K^2(alpha^2 + tfrac8sqrtM(normE[z_ell-1^2]_infty + K^2 a_ell - 2)) \\ &le alpha^2 + 48(1 lor K^2)a_ell - 1 + 6(1 lor 8M^-1/2)K^2(alpha^2 + normE[z_ell-1^2]_infty + K^2 a_ell - 2) \\ &le alpha^2 + 48(1 lor K^2)a_ell - 1 + 6(1 lor 8M^-1/2)K^2(a_ell - 1 + K^2 a_ell - 2) \\ &le alpha^2 + (48 + 6(1 lor 8M^-1/2))(1 lor K^2)a_ell - 1 + 6(1 lor 8M^-1/2) (1 lor K^4) a_ell - 2 \\ &le (48 + 6(1 lor 8M^-1/2) )(1 lor K^2)a_ell - 1 + (1 + 6(1 lor 8M^-1/2)) (1 lor K^4) a_ell - 2 . nodes.statement: The proof of this lemma uses exactly the same approach as creflem:outer. Set z_1' &= z_1 - tfrac1sqrtM_2E[W] (phi_2 + alpha)(z_2) - E[b]. Consider absE[phi_1(z_1,m) phi_1(z_1,m')] &le sqrtE[(phi_1(z_1,m) - phi_1(z'_1,m))^2] E[phi^2_1(z_1,m')] + absE[phi_1(z'_1,m) phi_1(z_1,m')] \\ &le sqrtab +absE[phi_1(z'_1,m) phi_1(z_1,m')] where we denote a = normE[z^2_1]_infty, b = normE[(z_1 - z'_1)^2]_infty. Similarly, absE[phi_1(z'_1,m) phi_1(z_1,m')] &le sqrt E[phi^2_1(z'_1,m)] E[(phi_1(z_1,m') - phi_1(z'_1,m'))^2] + absE[phi_1(z'_1,m) phi_1(z'_1,m')]. By subtracting and adding E_Q[w_L+1]E_Q[w_L+1]^T + I, we have abstr left( E_Q[w_L+1 w_L+1^T] A right) &= abstr left( (Sigma_Q - I + E_Q[w_L+1]E_Q[w_L+1]^T + I) A right) \\ &= abstr left( (Sigma_Q - I)A + E_Q[w_L+1]E_Q[w_L+1]^T A + A right) \\ &le abstr left( (Sigma_Q - I)A right) + abstr left(E_Q[w_L+1]E_Q[w_L+1]^T Aright) + abstr left( A right). We deal with each of the three terms in crefeqn:tr_ww_A separately. Consider the first term in crefeqn:tr_ww_A, since Sigma_Q - I = diag(bmupsigma_Q^2 - 1) is a diagonal matrix, by Cauchy-Schwarz abstr left( (Sigma_Q - I)A right) &= abslangle bmupsigma_Q^2 - 1, E_Q[phi^2(z_L)] - E_P[phi^2(z_L)] rangle \\ &le normbmupsigma_Q^2 - 1_2 normE_Q[phi^2(z_L)] - E_P[phi^2(z_L)]_2 \\ &oversetsmash(i)le left( (2+K)K right) left( 8 sqrt2 rho_alpha, M^L-tfrac12 L^1/2 K (K^2 lor 1)^L-tfrac12left(alpha^2 + 1lor tfrac1Dssi\|x\|^2_2right) right) \\ &oversetsmash(ii)le 32 sqrt2 rho_alpha, M^L-tfrac12 L^1/2 K (K^2 lor 1)^L+tfrac12left(alpha^2 + 1lor tfrac1Dssi\|x\|^2_2right), where in (i) we use creflem:parameter_bound and creflem:diag-frob-norm (proved later) while in (ii) we use 2+K le 2(1+K) le 4 (Klor 1) = 4 (K^2lor 1)^1/2 and K le K lor 1 = (K^2 lor 1)^1/2. Next, consider the second term in crefeqn:tr_ww_A, since tr(u v^T) = v^T u for u, v in R^M, abstr left(E_Q[w_L+1]E_Q[w_L+1]^T Aright) &= absE_Q[w_L+1]^T A E_Q[w_L+1] \\ &le normE_Q[w_L+1]_2^2 normA_2 \\ &le K^2 normA_2, where the first inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz and the definition of the operator norm while the second inequality follows from creflem:parameter_bound. Putting in the bound on normA_2, a bound on the second term in crefeqn:tr_ww_A is abstr left(E_Q[w_L+1]E_Q[w_L+1]^T Aright) &le 48sqrtM K^2 left(gamma_alpha,M(K^2 lor 1)right)^Lleft(alpha^2 + 1lor tfrac1Dssi\|x\|^2_2right) \\ &le 48sqrtM gamma_alpha,M^L K (K^2 lor 1)^L+tfrac12left(alpha^2 + 1lor tfrac1Dssi\|x\|^2_2right), where we use K le K lor 1 = (K^2 lor 1)^1/2 Finally, consider the third term in crefeqn:tr_ww_A. nodes.statement: We would like to combine the two expectations into a single expectation. First, note that Sigma_Q - I is a diagonal matrix and let bmupsigma^2 = diag(Sigma_Q). Since the trace of a matrix product is the element-wise inner product of the matrices, the first term in crefeq:diag_trace_term becomes leftlverttrparens* parens*Sigma_Q- IE_ensuremathQ[phisso(z_L)phisso(z_L)^T] rightrvert &= leftlvertlangle bmupsigma_Q^2 - 1, E_ensuremathQ[phisso^2(z_L)]]rangle rightrvert \\ &leq \|bmupsigma_Q^2 - 1\|_1\|E_ensuremathQ[phisso^2(z_L) ] \|_infty \\ &leq sqrtM \|bmupsigma_Q^2 - 1\|_2 \|E_ensuremathQ[phisso^2(z_L)]\|_infty where the first inequality is an application of H\"older's inequality. Now \|bmupsigma_Q^2 -1\|_2 leq left (2 + Kright)K by creflem:parameter_bound (iv.), where K = sqrt2KL(ensuremathQ,ensuremathP). To upper bound normE_Q[phi^2(z_L)]_infty, notice we can use the oddness and Lipschitz property of phisso to write normE[phisso^2(z^Q_L)]_infty = normE[(phisso(z^Q_L) - phisso(0))^2]_infty le normE[(z^Q_L)^2]_infty. nodes.statement: For a Student t likelihood (used in robust regression) with nu >0 degrees of freedom, we have log p(y_n |f(x_n)) = c(nu) - fracnu+12 log parens*1+frac(f(x_n)-y_n)^2nu. As the second term is non-negative, this is upper bounded by c(nu). Applying log (1+a) leq a, we have log p(y_n |f(x_n)) geq c(nu) - fracnu+12frac (f(x_n)-y_n)^2nu which provides the desired quadratic lower bound.

nodes.statement: For a logistic likelihood, we have log p(y_n |f(x_n)) = y_nlogparens*frac11+e^-f(x_n) + (1-y_n) logleft(frace^-f(x_n)1+e^-f(x_n)right) As both terms are non-positive, we have log p(y_n |f(x_n))leq 0. As g(a)=log(1+e^-a) is three times differentiable, we have that for any a in R, there exists a xi_a in R such that, log(1+e^-a) = log 2 - fraca2 + fraca^28 + fracg^(3)(xi_a)3!a^3. As sign(g^(3)(xi_a)) = sign(xi_a) =sign(a) = sign(a^3), the final term is non-negative, so log(1+e^-a) leq log 2 - fraca2 + fraca^28. Hence log p(y_n=1 |f(x_n)) &geq -log 2 + fracf(x_n) 2-fracf(x_n) ^28 and \\ log p(y_n=0 |f(x_n)) &= log p(y_n=1 |f(x_n))-f(x_n) geq -log 2 -fracf(x_n) 2-fracf(x_n) ^28.

nodes.statement: The proof conceptually proceeds in two steps. In the first conceptual step, we show that the parameters of all layers but the last layer converge to the prior. Intuitively, this means that the overall solution converges to mean-field inference in the Bayesian linear regression model with features x mapsto E[phi(z_L,m)(x)]. In the second conceptual step, we show that this mean-field solution of the Bayesian linear regression model converges to the prior, thereby completing the proof. Whereas conceptually the proof proceeds in two steps, below we split up these two steps into six steps, as follows: [leftmargin=5em] item[Step 1:] We prove that the parameters of the hidden layers converge to the prior. item[Step 2:] By assuming two claims, Claim 1 and Claim 2, we almost conclude the proof. It only remains to compute the limiting distribution of the final bias. item[Step 3:] We prove Claim 1. item[Step 4:] Using Claim 1, we compute the limiting distribution of the final bias. item[Step 5:] Using Claim 1 and the limiting distribution of the final bias, we prove Claim 2. item[Step 6:] We reconcile Step 2 with the limiting distribution of the bias to finally conclude the proof. Throughout the proof and unlike in the theorem statement, we do not incorporate alpha in phi, but write phi_alpha = phi + alpha for the version of phi that does include alpha. Moreover, we write bmuptheta_L+1 for the parameters of the final layer and let bmuptheta_1:L be all remaining parameters, so bmuptheta = (bmuptheta_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). We decompose the parameters of the final layer as bmuptheta_L+1 = (w_L+1, b_L+1), so also bmuptheta = (w_L+1, b_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). We will consider the limits M to infty and KL to 0. Using results from earlier sections in the appendix, we establish the following bounds which ignore proportionality constants irrelevant for the limits M to infty and KL to 0: normE_Q[phi(z_L+1)]_2 overset(creflem:last-layer-bound)&lesssim\!\!\!\!\! sqrtKL(Q_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L), \\ absE_Q[tfrac1sqrtM lraw_L+1, phi(z_L+1)] overset(crefthm:app-convergence-of-mean)&lesssim\!\!\!\!\! tfrac1sqrtM KL(Q_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L, P_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L), \\ absE_Q[b_L+1] overset(creflem:parameter_bound)&lesssim sqrtKL(Q_b_L+1, P_b_L+1), \\ tfrac1M normE_Q[phi(z_L)phi(z_L)^T]_2 overset(creflem:offdiag-operator-norm)&lesssim tfrac1sqrtM, \\ normE_Q[phi_alpha(z_L)^2]_infty overset(creflem:z-squared-recursion)&lesssim 1, \\ absE_Q[phi(z_L,m)phi(z_L,m')] overset(creflem:cov,lem:z-squared-recursion, m neq m')&lesssim sqrtKL(Q_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L), \\ \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!tfrac1Mabstr left( E_Q[w_L+1 w_L+1^T] ( E_Q[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] \!-\! E_P[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] ) right) overset(creflem:second_moment_conditional_prior)&lesssim tfrac1sqrtM sqrtKL(Q_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L,\! P_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L), \\ tfrac1MabsE[lraw_L+1, alpha 1 lraw_L+1, phi(z_L)] overset(creflem:inner_prod)&lesssim tfrac1sqrtM sqrtKL(Q_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L, P_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). Recall that any KL divergence between parameters of an optimal variational posterior and the prior is bounded uniformly over M (crefapp:kl-bounds). This means, e.g., that the mean of any weight of any variational posterior can be considered as an unknown but bounded constant (crefapp:parameter-bounds). Step 1 (convergence of hidden layers). Let P be the prior and let Q^* be the optimal mean-field posterior. Decompose the KL divergence as follows: KL(Q^*, P) = KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_L+1, P_bmuptheta_L+1) + KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) = E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - ELBO(Q^*). Let Q' be the modification of Q^* where the distribution of bmuptheta_1:L is set to the prior. Then KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) &= E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - ELBO(Q^*) - KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_L+1, P_bmuptheta_L+1) \\ &= E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - ELBO(Q^*) + ELBO(Q') - E_Q'[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)]. Therefore, by optimality of Q^*, &KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) nonumber \\ & levphantomsum^N_n E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - E_Q'[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] \\ & = -frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^N( E_Q^*[(y_n - f(x_n))^2] - E_Q'[(y_n - f(x_n))^2] ) \\ & = -frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^N( E_Q^*[f^2(x_n) - 2 y_n f(x_n) ] - E_Q^*[E_P[f^2(x_n) - 2 y_n f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] ) \\ & le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig( absE_Q^*[f^2(x_n) -E_P[f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] + 2 absy_n absE_Q^*[f(x_n) -E_P[f(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] Big). Define tilde b = tfrac1sqrtMlraw_L+1, alpha 1 + b_L+1 and let tilde f(x_n) = f(x_n) - tilde b. Note that tilde b is sigma(bmuptheta_L+1)-measurable (i.e.~tilde b is deterministic after conditioning on the top layer parameters). Rearrange as &E_Q^*[f^2(x_n) -E_P[f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] nonumber \\ & = E_Q^*[ tilde f^2(x_n) + 2 tilde b tilde f(x_n) + tilde b^2 -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n) + 2 tilde b tilde f(x_n) + tilde b^2\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1] ] \\ & = E_Q^*[ tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1] ] + 2\, E_Q^*[tilde b (tilde f(x_n) - E_P[tilde f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1])]. This gives &KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) nonumber \\ & le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig( absE_Q^*[tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] + 2 absy_n absE_Q^*[tilde f(x_n) -E_P[tilde f(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] nonumber \\ &hphantom le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig(\; + 2\, absE_Q^*[tilde b (tilde f(x_n) - E_P[tilde f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1])] Big). By oddness of phi, it can be seen that E_P[tilde f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1] = 0. Therefore, &KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) nonumber \\ & le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig( absE_Q^*[tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] + 2 absy_n absE_Q^*[tilde f(x_n)] + 2 absE_Q^*[tilde b tilde f(x_n)] Big). Here E_Q^*[tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] &= tfrac1Mtr E_Q^*[w_L+1 w_L+1^T] ( E_Q^*[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] - E_P[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] ), which is O(1/sqrtM) by crefeq:dist:complicated_trace, and absE_Q^*[tilde b tilde f(x_n)] &le absE_Q^*[b_L+1] absE_Q^*[tilde f(x_n)] + tfrac1MabsE_Q^*[lraw_L+1, alpha 1 lraw_L+1, phi(z_L)], which is O(1/sqrtM) by crefeq:dist:bias,eq:dist:mean applied to the first term and crefeq:dist:complicated_inner_prod applied to the second term. Therefore, KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) = O(1/sqrtM). Step 2 (beginning of conclusion of proof). Let d_M = sum_n=1^N (y_n - E_Q^*[b_L+1]). Although d_M depends on Q^*_b_L+1 which in turn depends on M, note that E_Q^*[b_L+1] and therefore d_M can be treated like unknown but bounded constants. Set c_M = fracalpha d_Malpha^2 N + sigma^2. We make two claims: KL(Q^*_w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1, P_w_L+1) &to 0, tagClaim 1 \\ c_M &to c_infty tagClaim 2 where Q^*_w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1 is the distribution of w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1 under Q^* and c_infty in R is some constant. The claims will be proven in the next parts. Assuming the claims, denote w_L+1' = w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1 and phi_alpha = phi + alpha and decompose tfrac1sqrtMlraw_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) &= tfrac1sqrtMlraw'_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) + tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L). By Chebyshev's inequality, we have tfracc_MM lra1, phi(z_L) to 0 in probability under Q^*: E_Q^*[tfrac1M lra1, phi(z_L)] &le tfrac1sqrtM normE_Q^*[phi(z_L)]_2 \\ V_Q^*[tfrac1Mlra1, phi(z_L)] &= tfrac1M^2 lra1, E_Q^*[phi(z_L)phi(z_L)^T] 1 - tfrac1M^2 lra1, E_Q^*[phi(z_L)]^2 \\ &le tfrac1M normE_Q^*[phi(z_L)phi(z_L)^T]_2 + tfrac1M normE_Q^*[phi(z_L)]_2^2, which are both O(1/sqrtM) using crefeq:dist:phi,eq:dist:outer. Since tfracc_MM lra1, phi(z_L) to 0 in probability, tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L) = tfracc_MM lra1, phi(z_L) + alpha c_M to alpha c_infty in probability by Claim 2. Suppressing the dependence on x, define g_bmuptheta = tfrac1sqrtMlraw'_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) and note that it is a deterministic function of (w'_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). Also write f_bmuptheta = tfrac1sqrtMlraw_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) and note that it the same deterministic function of (w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). (That it is the same deterministic function will allow us to use the data processing inequality below.) Let I in N and X = (x_1, ldots, x_I) in (R^Dssi)^I. Let Q^(M)_g be the finite-dimensional distribution of g at X under the optimal mean-field solution Q^* at width M and let P^(M)_f be the finite-dimensional distribution of f at X under the prior P at width M. Using Pinsker's inequality and the data processing inequality for KL-divergences we have TV(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) leq sqrttfrac12KL(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) leq sqrttfrac12KL(ensuremathQ^(M)_w'_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L,ensuremathP^(M)_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L), which goes to zero as M to infty by the previous part and Claim 1. Let d be the L\'evy--Prokhorov metric on R^I with the Borel sigma-algebra. Since R^I is separable, the L\'evy--Prokhorov metric metrizes weak convergence. Moreover, since R^I is separable, the L\'evy--Prokhorov metric is upper bounded by the total variation distance. By triangle inequality we then bound the distance between Q^(M)_g and the NNGP, which we denote by PssNN: d(Q^(M)_g, PssNN) leq d(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) + d(P^(M)_f, PssNN) leq TV(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) + d(P^(M)_f, PssNN). As M to infty, the first term converges to zero by crefeqn:pinsker0 and the second term converges to zero because P_f^(M) converges to the NNGP citepmatthews_2018. Hence, Q^(M)_g converges weakly to the NNGP, PssNN. Since f = g + tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L) and we previously showed that tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L) to alpha c_infty in probability under Q^*, we conclude that, along any finite-dimensional distribution, f converges to the NNGP plus the constant alpha c_infty. It remains to add the limiting distribution of the bias, which we do in the last step of the proof. Step 3 (proof of Claim 1). We previously claimed that KL(Q^*_w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1, P_w_L+1) to 0. We now prove this claim. Let q^*(bmuptheta) = q^*(w_L+1)q^*(b_L+1)q^*(bmuptheta_1:L) be the density of Q^* w.r.t.\ the Lebesgue measure. Let L(q(w_L+1),q(b_L+1),q(bmuptheta_1:L)) be the ELBO: &L(q(w_L+1),q(b_L+1),q(bmuptheta_1:L)) nonumber \\ & = E_q[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - KL(q(w_L+1),p(w_L+1)) - KL(q(b_L+1),p(b_L+1)) - KL(q(bmuptheta_1:L),p(bmuptheta_1:L)). Because Q^* is optimal, q^*(w_L+1) maximizes the function q(w_L+1) mapsto L(q(w_L+1),q^*(b_L+1),q^*(bmuptheta_1:L)). We therefore parametrize q(w_L+1) = N(bmupmu, diag(bmupnu)) and set the gradients of (bmupmu, bmupnu) mapsto L(q(w_L+1),q^*(b_L+1),q^*(bmuptheta_1:L)) to zero to find equations which characterize the mean and variance of q^*(w_L+1) = N(bmupmu^*, diag(bmupnu^*)). Consider the joint density q(bmuptheta) = q(w_L+1)q^*(b_L+1)q^*(bmuptheta_1:L). Denote phi_alpha = phi + alpha. Compute &E_q[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - KL(q(w_L+1),p(w_L+1)) nonumber \\ &\; = -frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^N parens* tfrac1Mlra bmupmu bmupmu^T + diag(bmupnu), E_Q^*[phi_alpha(z_L)phi_alpha(z_L)^T] - 2 tfrac1sqrtMlra bmupmu, E_Q^*[(y_n - b_L+1)phi_alpha(z_L)] + E_Q^*[y_n - b_L+1]^2 nonumber\\ & - frac12 normbmupmu_2^2 - frac12 sum_m=1^M(nu_m - 1 - log(nu_m)). Denote A = frac1M sum_n=1^N E_Q^*[phi_alpha(z_L(x_n))phi_alpha(z_L(x_n))^T], b = frac1sqrtMsum_n=1^N(y_n - E_q[b_L+1]) E_Q^*[phi_alpha(z_L(x_n))]. Then the part of the ELBO depending on bmupmu and bmupnu can be written as -frac12sigma^2 sbrac* lra bmupmu bmupmu^T + diag(bmupnu), A - 2 lra bmupmu, b + (y_n - E_Q^*[b_L+1])^2 - frac12 normbmupmu_2^2 - frac12 sum_m=1^M(nu_m - 1 - log(nu_m)). Setting the gradient with respect to bmupmu to zero gives -frac1sigma^2A bmupmu^* + frac1sigma^2b - bmupmu^* = 0 implies bmupmu^* = (A + sigma^2 I)^-1b. Similarly, setting the gradient with respect nu_m to zero gives -frac12sigma^2 A_mm - frac12 + frac12frac1nu_m^* = 0 implies nu_m^* = frac11 + frac1sigma^2A_mm. Therefore, KL(Q^*_w_L+1 - tfracc_MsqrtM 1, P_w_L+1) &= frac12 normbmupmu^* - tfracc_MsqrtM 1_2^2 + frac12sum_m=1^M (nu_m^* - 1 - log(nu_m^*)) \\ &= frac12 sigma^2 normbmupmu^* - tfracc_MsqrtM 1_2^2 + frac12 sum_m=1^Mparens* log(1 + tfrac1sigma^2A_mm) - fractfrac1sigma^2A_mm1 + tfrac1sigma^2A_mm \\ &overset(i)le frac12 sigma^2 normbmupmu^* - tfracc_MsqrtM 1_2^2 + frac12 Mparens* log(1 + tfrac1MtfracMsigma^2A_m^*) - fractfrac1MtfracMsigma^2A_m^*1 + tfrac1MtfracMsigma^2A_m^* \\ &overset(ii)le frac12 sigma^2 normbmupmu^* - tfracc_MsqrtM 1_2^2 + frac12 sigma^2 fracMsigma^2A^2_m^* where in (i) A_m^* = relax_m in [M] A_mm and we use that a - 1 - log(a) is increasing in a for a<1 and that nu^*_m<1. nodes.clean_text: The proof conceptually proceeds in two steps. In the first conceptual step, we show that the parameters of all layers but the last layer converge to the prior. Intuitively, this means that the overall solution converges to mean-field inference in the Bayesian linear regression model with features x mapsto E[phi(z_L,m)(x)]. In the second conceptual step, we show that this mean-field solution of the Bayesian linear regression model converges to the prior, thereby completing the proof. Whereas conceptually the proof proceeds in two steps, below we split up these two steps into six steps, as follows: [leftmargin=5em] item[Step 1:] We prove that the parameters of the hidden layers converge to the prior. item[Step 2:] By assuming two claims, Claim 1 and Claim 2, we almost conclude the proof. It only remains to compute the limiting distribution of the final bias. item[Step 3:] We prove Claim 1. item[Step 4:] Using Claim 1, we compute the limiting distribution of the final bias. item[Step 5:] Using Claim 1 and the limiting distribution of the final bias, we prove Claim 2. item[Step 6:] We reconcile Step 2 with the limiting distribution of the bias to finally conclude the proof. Throughout the proof and unlike in the theorem statement, we do not incorporate alpha in phi, but write phi_alpha = phi + alpha for the version of phi that does include alpha. Moreover, we write bmuptheta_L+1 for the parameters of the final layer and let bmuptheta_1:L be all remaining parameters, so bmuptheta = (bmuptheta_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). We decompose the parameters of the final layer as bmuptheta_L+1 = (w_L+1, b_L+1), so also bmuptheta = (w_L+1, b_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). We will consider the limits M to infty and KL to 0. Using results from earlier sections in the appendix, we establish the following bounds which ignore proportionality constants irrelevant for the limits M to infty and KL to 0: normE_Q[phi(z_L+1)]_2 overset(creflem:last-layer-bound)&lesssim\!\!\!\!\! sqrtKL(Q_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L), \\ absE_Q[tfrac1sqrtM lraw_L+1, phi(z_L+1)] overset(crefthm:app-convergence-of-mean)&lesssim\!\!\!\!\! tfrac1sqrtM KL(Q_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L, P_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L), \\ absE_Q[b_L+1] overset(creflem:parameter_bound)&lesssim sqrtKL(Q_b_L+1, P_b_L+1), \\ tfrac1M normE_Q[phi(z_L)phi(z_L)^T]_2 overset(creflem:offdiag-operator-norm)&lesssim tfrac1sqrtM, \\ normE_Q[phi_alpha(z_L)^2]_infty overset(creflem:z-squared-recursion)&lesssim 1, \\ absE_Q[phi(z_L,m)phi(z_L,m')] overset(creflem:cov,lem:z-squared-recursion, m neq m')&lesssim sqrtKL(Q_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L), \\ \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!tfrac1Mabstr left( E_Q[w_L+1 w_L+1^T] ( E_Q[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] \!-\! E_P[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] ) right) overset(creflem:second_moment_conditional_prior)&lesssim tfrac1sqrtM sqrtKL(Q_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L,\! P_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L), \\ tfrac1MabsE[lraw_L+1, alpha 1 lraw_L+1, phi(z_L)] overset(creflem:inner_prod)&lesssim tfrac1sqrtM sqrtKL(Q_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L, P_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). Recall that any KL divergence between parameters of an optimal variational posterior and the prior is bounded uniformly over M (crefapp:kl-bounds). This means, e.g., that the mean of any weight of any variational posterior can be considered as an unknown but bounded constant (crefapp:parameter-bounds). Step 1 (convergence of hidden layers). Let P be the prior and let Q^* be the optimal mean-field posterior. Decompose the KL divergence as follows: KL(Q^*, P) = KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_L+1, P_bmuptheta_L+1) + KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) = E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - ELBO(Q^*). Let Q' be the modification of Q^* where the distribution of bmuptheta_1:L is set to the prior. Then KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) &= E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - ELBO(Q^*) - KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_L+1, P_bmuptheta_L+1) \\ &= E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - ELBO(Q^*) + ELBO(Q') - E_Q'[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)]. Therefore, by optimality of Q^*, &KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) nonumber \\ & levphantomsum^N_n E_Q^*[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - E_Q'[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] \\ & = -frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^N( E_Q^*[(y_n - f(x_n))^2] - E_Q'[(y_n - f(x_n))^2] ) \\ & = -frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^N( E_Q^*[f^2(x_n) - 2 y_n f(x_n) ] - E_Q^*[E_P[f^2(x_n) - 2 y_n f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] ) \\ & le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig( absE_Q^*[f^2(x_n) -E_P[f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] + 2 absy_n absE_Q^*[f(x_n) -E_P[f(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] Big). Define tilde b = tfrac1sqrtMlraw_L+1, alpha 1 + b_L+1 and let tilde f(x_n) = f(x_n) - tilde b. Note that tilde b is sigma(bmuptheta_L+1)-measurable (i.e.~tilde b is deterministic after conditioning on the top layer parameters). Rearrange as &E_Q^*[f^2(x_n) -E_P[f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] nonumber \\ & = E_Q^*[ tilde f^2(x_n) + 2 tilde b tilde f(x_n) + tilde b^2 -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n) + 2 tilde b tilde f(x_n) + tilde b^2\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1] ] \\ & = E_Q^*[ tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1] ] + 2\, E_Q^*[tilde b (tilde f(x_n) - E_P[tilde f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1])]. This gives &KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) nonumber \\ & le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig( absE_Q^*[tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] + 2 absy_n absE_Q^*[tilde f(x_n) -E_P[tilde f(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] nonumber \\ &hphantom le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig(\; + 2\, absE_Q^*[tilde b (tilde f(x_n) - E_P[tilde f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1])] Big). By oddness of phi, it can be seen that E_P[tilde f(x_n) \,|\, bmuptheta_L+1] = 0. Therefore, &KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) nonumber \\ & le frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^NBig( absE_Q^*[tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] + 2 absy_n absE_Q^*[tilde f(x_n)] + 2 absE_Q^*[tilde b tilde f(x_n)] Big). Here E_Q^*[tilde f^2(x_n) -E_P[tilde f^2(x_n)\,|\, bmuptheta_L+1]] &= tfrac1Mtr E_Q^*[w_L+1 w_L+1^T] ( E_Q^*[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] - E_P[phi(z_L) phi(z_L)^T] ), which is O(1/sqrtM) by crefeq:dist:complicated_trace, and absE_Q^*[tilde b tilde f(x_n)] &le absE_Q^*[b_L+1] absE_Q^*[tilde f(x_n)] + tfrac1MabsE_Q^*[lraw_L+1, alpha 1 lraw_L+1, phi(z_L)], which is O(1/sqrtM) by crefeq:dist:bias,eq:dist:mean applied to the first term and crefeq:dist:complicated_inner_prod applied to the second term. Therefore, KL(Q^*_bmuptheta_1:L, P_bmuptheta_1:L) = O(1/sqrtM). Step 2 (beginning of conclusion of proof). Let d_M = sum_n=1^N (y_n - E_Q^*[b_L+1]). Although d_M depends on Q^*_b_L+1 which in turn depends on M, note that E_Q^*[b_L+1] and therefore d_M can be treated like unknown but bounded constants. Set c_M = fracalpha d_Malpha^2 N + sigma^2. We make two claims: KL(Q^*_w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1, P_w_L+1) &to 0, tagClaim 1 \\ c_M &to c_infty tagClaim 2 where Q^*_w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1 is the distribution of w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1 under Q^* and c_infty in R is some constant. The claims will be proven in the next parts. Assuming the claims, denote w_L+1' = w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1 and phi_alpha = phi + alpha and decompose tfrac1sqrtMlraw_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) &= tfrac1sqrtMlraw'_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) + tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L). By Chebyshev's inequality, we have tfracc_MM lra1, phi(z_L) to 0 in probability under Q^*: E_Q^*[tfrac1M lra1, phi(z_L)] &le tfrac1sqrtM normE_Q^*[phi(z_L)]_2 \\ V_Q^*[tfrac1Mlra1, phi(z_L)] &= tfrac1M^2 lra1, E_Q^*[phi(z_L)phi(z_L)^T] 1 - tfrac1M^2 lra1, E_Q^*[phi(z_L)]^2 \\ &le tfrac1M normE_Q^*[phi(z_L)phi(z_L)^T]_2 + tfrac1M normE_Q^*[phi(z_L)]_2^2, which are both O(1/sqrtM) using crefeq:dist:phi,eq:dist:outer. Since tfracc_MM lra1, phi(z_L) to 0 in probability, tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L) = tfracc_MM lra1, phi(z_L) + alpha c_M to alpha c_infty in probability by Claim 2. Suppressing the dependence on x, define g_bmuptheta = tfrac1sqrtMlraw'_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) and note that it is a deterministic function of (w'_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). Also write f_bmuptheta = tfrac1sqrtMlraw_L+1, phi_alpha(z_L) and note that it the same deterministic function of (w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L). (That it is the same deterministic function will allow us to use the data processing inequality below.) Let I in N and X = (x_1, ldots, x_I) in (R^Dssi)^I. Let Q^(M)_g be the finite-dimensional distribution of g at X under the optimal mean-field solution Q^* at width M and let P^(M)_f be the finite-dimensional distribution of f at X under the prior P at width M. Using Pinsker's inequality and the data processing inequality for KL-divergences we have TV(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) leq sqrttfrac12KL(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) leq sqrttfrac12KL(ensuremathQ^(M)_w'_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L,ensuremathP^(M)_w_L+1, bmuptheta_1:L), which goes to zero as M to infty by the previous part and Claim 1. Let d be the L\'evy--Prokhorov metric on R^I with the Borel sigma-algebra. Since R^I is separable, the L\'evy--Prokhorov metric metrizes weak convergence. Moreover, since R^I is separable, the L\'evy--Prokhorov metric is upper bounded by the total variation distance. By triangle inequality we then bound the distance between Q^(M)_g and the NNGP, which we denote by PssNN: d(Q^(M)_g, PssNN) leq d(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) + d(P^(M)_f, PssNN) leq TV(Q^(M)_g, P^(M)_f) + d(P^(M)_f, PssNN). As M to infty, the first term converges to zero by crefeqn:pinsker0 and the second term converges to zero because P_f^(M) converges to the NNGP citepmatthews_2018. Hence, Q^(M)_g converges weakly to the NNGP, PssNN. Since f = g + tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L) and we previously showed that tfracc_MM lra1, phi_alpha(z_L) to alpha c_infty in probability under Q^*, we conclude that, along any finite-dimensional distribution, f converges to the NNGP plus the constant alpha c_infty. It remains to add the limiting distribution of the bias, which we do in the last step of the proof. Step 3 (proof of Claim 1). We previously claimed that KL(Q^*_w_L+1 - fracc_MsqrtM 1, P_w_L+1) to 0. We now prove this claim. Let q^*(bmuptheta) = q^*(w_L+1)q^*(b_L+1)q^*(bmuptheta_1:L) be the density of Q^* w.r.t.\ the Lebesgue measure. Let L(q(w_L+1),q(b_L+1),q(bmuptheta_1:L)) be the ELBO: &L(q(w_L+1),q(b_L+1),q(bmuptheta_1:L)) nonumber \\ & = E_q[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - KL(q(w_L+1),p(w_L+1)) - KL(q(b_L+1),p(b_L+1)) - KL(q(bmuptheta_1:L),p(bmuptheta_1:L)). Because Q^* is optimal, q^*(w_L+1) maximizes the function q(w_L+1) mapsto L(q(w_L+1),q^*(b_L+1),q^*(bmuptheta_1:L)). We therefore parametrize q(w_L+1) = N(bmupmu, diag(bmupnu)) and set the gradients of (bmupmu, bmupnu) mapsto L(q(w_L+1),q^*(b_L+1),q^*(bmuptheta_1:L)) to zero to find equations which characterize the mean and variance of q^*(w_L+1) = N(bmupmu^*, diag(bmupnu^*)). Consider the joint density q(bmuptheta) = q(w_L+1)q^*(b_L+1)q^*(bmuptheta_1:L). Denote phi_alpha = phi + alpha. Compute &E_q[log p(y \,|\, bmuptheta)] - KL(q(w_L+1),p(w_L+1)) nonumber \\ &\; = -frac12sigma^2sum_n=1^N parens* tfrac1Mlra bmupmu bmupmu^T + diag(bmupnu), E_Q^*[phi_alpha(z_L)phi_alpha(z_L)^T] - 2 tfrac1sqrtMlra bmupmu, E_Q^*[(y_n - b_L+1)phi_alpha(z_L)] + E_Q^*[y_n - b_L+1]^2 nonumber\\ & - frac12 normbmupmu_2^2 - frac12 sum_m=1^M(nu_m - 1 - log(nu_m)). Denote A = frac1M sum_n=1^N E_Q^*[phi_alpha(z_L(x_n))phi_alpha(z_L(x_n))^T], b = frac1sqrtMsum_n=1^N(y_n - E_q[b_L+1]) E_Q^*[phi_alpha(z_L(x_n))]. Then the part of the ELBO depending on bmupmu and bmupnu can be written as -frac12sigma^2 sbrac* lra bmupmu bmupmu^T + diag(bmupnu), A - 2 lra bmupmu, b + (y_n - E_Q^*[b_L+1])^2 - frac12 normbmupmu_2^2 - frac12 sum_m=1^M(nu_m - 1 - log(nu_m)). nodes.statement: We consider a Bayesian neural network prior with a standard Gaussian distribution over the weights defines in crefeqn:nn-output,eqn:nn-recursion,eqn:nn-base. Let Q denote the set of all mean field variational distributions over feed-forward neural networks with activation function phi, L hidden layers, and M neurons per layer. Assume the following conditions: [label=roman*.,itemsep=0pt,topsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt] item phi is continuous. item phi(a) = O(|a|+1). This condition is equivalent to the linear envelop condition citetmatthews_2018. item There exist a,a' in R such that phi_e(a) neq phi_e(a'). In words, it is not true that phi is equal to the sum of an odd function and a constant. item There exists an a in R such that phi(a)^2+phi(-a)^2 neq 2phi(0)^2. This is equivalent to phi^2 is not equal to an odd function plus a constant. For a dataset D=(x_n, y_n)ssn=1^N, with y_n in R^Dssi and a given homoscedastic Gaussian likelihood let ensuremathQ^* in Q be the optimal variational posterior for this dataset and likelihood. Then, there exists a dataset D and a homoscedastic Gaussian likelihood such that ensuremathQ^* satisfies |E_ensuremathQ^*[f_theta(x)]-E_ensuremathQ^*[f_theta(x')]| geq c where c is a constant independent of M.

\label{thm:app-counterexample}
 We consider a Bayesian neural network prior with a standard Gaussian distribution over the weights defines in \cref{eqn:nn-output,eqn:nn-recursion,eqn:nn-base}. Let $\mathcal{Q}$ denote the set of all mean field variational distributions over feed-forward neural networks with activation function $\phi$, $L$ hidden layers, and $M$ neurons per layer.
    Assume the following conditions:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\roman*.,itemsep=0pt,topsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt]
        \item $\phi$ is continuous.
        \item
            $\phi(a) = O(|a|+1)$.
            This condition is equivalent to the linear envelop condition \citet{matthews_2018}.
        \item There exist $a,a' \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\phi_e(a) \neq \phi_e(a')$. In words, it is not true that $\phi$ is equal to the sum of an odd function and a constant.
        \item There exists an $a \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\phi(a)^2+\phi(-a)^2 \neq 2\phi(0)^2$. This is equivalent to $\phi^2$ is not equal to an odd function plus a constant.
    \end{enumerate}
    For a dataset $D=(\mathbf{x}_n, y_n)\ss{n=1}^N$, with $y_n \in \mathbb{R}^{D\ss{i}}$ and a given homoscedastic Gaussian likelihood let $\ensuremath{Q}^* \in \mathcal{Q}$ be the optimal variational posterior for this dataset and likelihood.     \begin{align}
        |\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}^*}[f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})]-\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}^*}[f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}')]| \geq c
    \end{align}
    where $c$ is a constant independent of $M$.

Fix $\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^{D\ss{i}}$.
    Let $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, k^{L-1}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}))$ and let $\oto{\text{d}}$ denote convergence in distribution.
    By \citet[Theorem 4]{matthews_2018} under $\ensuremath{P}$, and hence also under $\ensuremath{Q}$, $z_{L-1,m}^M(\mathbf{x}) \oto{\text{d}} z$ for each $m$.
    Since $\phi$ is continuous, by the continuous mapping theorem \citep[Theorem 25.7]{billingsley2008probability}, $\phi(z_{L-1,m}^M(\mathbf{x})) \oto{\text{d}} \phi(z)$.
    To strengthen convergence in distribution to convergence of the means, we note that $(\phi(z_{L-1, m}^M(\mathbf{x})))_{M=1}^\infty$ is uniformly integrable \citep[Lemma 21 by][]{matthews_2018} and apply \citet[Theorem 25.12]{billingsley2008probability}:
    $\lambda_{M}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[\phi(z_{L-1,m}^M(\mathbf{x}))] \to \mathbb{E}[\phi(z)] = \lambda(\mathbf{x})$.
    Noting that $k^{L}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}) = 1 + \mathbb{E}[\phi(z)^2]$, the proof to show the second limit is exactly the same.

The existence of such an x, x' is guaranteed by crefprop:kernel-diagonal,lem:odd-fn1, see crefrem:combining-props. Choose y=sqrtClambda(x),y'=sqrtClambda(x') with Cin (0,infty) to be chosen later. We supress the dependce on C for convenience and write ensuremathQ:=ensuremathQ^C. Let ensuremathQ^* be any posterior with ELBO better than ensuremathQ, then frac12sigma^2&left(E_ensuremathQ^*[(y-f_theta(x))^2]+E_ensuremathQ^*[(y'-f_theta(x'))^2]right) \\ &leq KL(ensuremathQ,ensuremathP)- KL(ensuremathQ^*,ensuremathP) + frac12sigma^2left(E_ensuremathQ[(y-f_theta(x))^2]+E_ensuremathQ[(y'-f_theta(x'))^2]right) \\ & leq KL(ensuremathQ,ensuremathP) + frac12sigma^2left(E_ensuremathQ[(y-f_theta(x))^2]+E_ensuremathQ[(y'-f_theta(x'))^2]right) \\ & = fracC2 + frac12sigma^2left(E_ensuremathQ[(y-f_theta(x))^2]+E_ensuremathQ[(y'-f_theta(x'))^2]right). where the first inequality comes from rearranging both ELBOs, the second uses non-negativity of the KL divergence and makes use of crefprop:kl-to-prior. Using convexity of the squared function to apply Jensen's inequality to the left hand side, and multiplying both sides by 2sigma^2 we have, (y-E_ensuremathQ^*[f_theta(x)])^2+(y'-E_ensuremathQ^*[f_theta(x')])^2 & leq E_ensuremathQ^*[(y-f_theta(x))^2]+E_ensuremathQ^*[(y'-f_theta(x'))^2] \\ & leq sigma^2 C +E_ensuremathQ[(y-f_theta(x))^2]+E_ensuremathQ[(y'-f_theta(x'))^2]. Since lambda(x) neq lambda(x') there exists a beta>0 such that |lambda(x)-lambda(x')| geq beta/sqrt2. Using our choice of y,y' E_ensuremathQ^*[(y-f_theta(x))^2]&= E_ensuremathQ^*[sqrtClambda(x)-f_theta(x)]^2\\ & =(sqrtClambda(x)-sqrtClambda_M(x))^2+ kappa_M(x), where kappa_M is the variance function for the width M neural net prior. The same argument can be applied to x'. This gives us the upper bound, for M sufficiently large, E_ensuremathQ[(y-f_theta(x))^2]& leq kappa(x)+kappa(x') + beta^2. Combining with our earlier equation, we have (sqrtClambda(x)-E_ensuremathQ^*[f_theta(x)])^2+(sqrtClambda(x')-E_ensuremathQ^*[f_theta(x')])^2 leq sigma^2C + kappa(x) + kappa(x') + beta^2. nodes.statement: Let (a_i)_i ge 1 subseteq R be convergent to some a in R. We show that E[phi(a_i z)] to E[phi(a z)]. If we can interchange limit and expectation, then the result follows from continuity of phi. To show that we can interchange limit and expectation, we demonstrate an integrable dominating function. Since (a_i)_i ge 1 is convergent, it is bounded, hence contained in some interval [-K, K] subseteq R. Using that phi(a) = O(|a|+1), let |phi(a)| le C |a| for all |a| ge R for some C > 0. Let M be the maximum of |phi| on [-R, R], which is finite because |phi| is continuous. Then estimate |phi(a_i z)| le relax_a in [-K, K] |phi(a z)| le M + C relax_a in [-K, K] |a z| le M + C K |z|, which is integrable because z sim N(0,1).
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $(a_i)_{i \ge 1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be convergent to some $a \in \mathbb{R}$.
    We show that $\mathbb{E}[\phi(a_i z)] \to \mathbb{E}[\phi(a z)]$.
    If we can interchange limit and expectation, then the result follows from continuity of $\phi$.
    To show that we can interchange limit and expectation, we demonstrate an integrable dominating function.
    Since $(a_i)_{i \ge 1}$ is convergent, it is bounded, hence contained in some interval $[-K, K] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.
    Using that $\phi(a) = O(|a|+1)$, let $|\phi(a)| \le C |a|$ for all $|a| \ge R$ for some $C > 0$.
    Let $M$ be the maximum of $|\phi|$ on $[-R, R]$, which is finite because $|\phi|$ is continuous.
    Then estimate
    \begin{equation}
        |\phi(a_i z)|
        \le \relax_{a \in [-K, K]} |\phi(a z)|
        \le M + C \relax_{a \in [-K, K]} |a z|
        \le M + C K |z|,
    \end{equation}
    which is integrable because $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{lem:odd-fn1}
nodes.statement: Our proof follows citetStackExchangeGaussiansDense. Without loss of generality, we may assume I=(s,t) is bounded with s>0. Towards contradiction, suppose there exists a c in R such that alpha(a)=c for all a in I. This supposition can be written as, int phi(az) e^-z^2/2 dz = c' forall a in I, where c' = csqrt2pi. Define u = az, b = 1/(2a^2) and I'= left(frac12t^2, frac12s^2right). Then we can rewrite crefeqn:constant-expectation as int phi(u) e^-bu^2 du = c' forall b in I'. We have |u^2nphi(u)e^-bu^2|leq u^2n|phi(u)|e^-bu^2 leq u^2n|phi(u)|e^-fracu^22t^2, which is integrable since phi(u)=O(|x|+1). Hence we may take n derivatives and apply Leibniz's rule, fracpartial^npartial^n b int phi(u) e^-bu^2 du = int u^2n phi(u) e^-bu^2 du = 0 forall b in I', forall n in N. For a (arbitrary) b in I', define w(u) = e^-bu^2 and L^2(R, w) to be the Hilbert space with inner product langle f,g rangle = int f(u)g(u)w(u)du. Following citet126471, we note that the set of compactly supported functions is dense in L^2(R, w), and by the Weirstrauss theorem the set of polynomial is dense in the set of compact functions. As a dense subset of a dense set is again dense, we conclude the set of polynomial is dense in L^2(R, w). Writing phi(u) = phi_e(u) + phi_o(u), we have, int_-infty^infty u^2i-1 phi_e(u) w(u) du &= 0 forall i in N as the integrand is odd and we integrate over a symmetric domain. Also, int u^2n fracphi(u)+ phi(-u)2w(u) du &= frac12int u^2i phi(u)w(u) du + frac12int u^2n phi(-u)w(u) du \\ &=frac12int u^2i phi(u)w(u) du + frac12int u^2n phi(u)w(u) du \\ &=0 + 0, forall i in N, by crefeqn:orthogonal-even. Since the polynomial are a basis, we have phi_e(u) = sum_i=0^infty alpha_i u^i for some (alpha_i)_i=1^infty. Taking the inner product of both sides with respect to u^i, shows that alpha_i=0 for all i >0, hence phi_e(u)= c^primeprime for some c^primeprime in R, with equality in L^2(R,w). But as phi_e is continuous, this implies it is equal to a c^primeprime everywhere. As I contains an open set, it contains a ball. As alpha is continuous (crefprop:e-is-continuous) the image of this ball under alpha is connected i.e.~an interval. As the interval contains at least two points, it contains an open interval.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{prop:kernel-diagonal}
nodes.statement: The proof proceeds by induction. paragraphBase case: We have kappa^0(x) = 1+ \|x\|^2_2. As R^Dssi contains an open set, it contains an open ball. The image of this open ball under the map kappa, which is continuous, must be connected, hence an interval. Therefore, if it contains at least two points, it contains an open interval. But in any ball, there are two points with different norms, so this must be the case. paragraphInductive step: Defining h(a) = E[phi(az)] and following the recursion for kernels for deep networks citet[Lemma 2]matthews_2018, we have kappa^ell(R^Dssi) = 1+ h(kappa^ell-1(R^Dssi)). By the inductive hypothesis, kappa^ell-1(R^Dssi) contains an open interval, I, the image of which must be connected as h is continuous (phi^2 is continuous and is O(|a|^2+1) so we may apply crefprop:e-is-continuous). Hence, it suffices to show that phi^2 satisfies the conditions of creflem:odd-fn1. This follows from the assumption that phi(a)^2+phi(-a^2) neq c.

Assume the following:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),topsep=0pt]
        \item $D\ss{o} = 1$.
        \item $\phi$ is a sum of an odd function and a constant: $\phi\ss{e}$ is constant.
        \item $\phi$ is twice continuously differentiable with $\norm{\phi'}_\infty \le 1$ and $\norm{\phi''}_\infty < \infty$.
        \item $\phi^2$ is not a sum of an odd function and a constant: $\phi^2(a) + \phi^2(-a) \neq 2 \phi^2(0)$ for some $a \in \mathbb{R}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then, if $\phi\ss{o}$ is non-linear, there exist two inputs $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}' \in \mathbb{R}^{D\ss{i}}$ and a constant $c > 0$ such that, for every $K > 0$, there exists a sequence of mean-field distributions $(\ensuremath{Q}_M)_{M \ge 1}$ with $\operatorname{KL}(\ensuremath{Q}_M, \ensuremath{P}) = K $, one for every network width $M \ge 1$, that achieves
    \begin{equation}
        \lim_{M \to \infty} \sqrt{M}\abs{\mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}_M}[f(\mathbf{x})] - \mathbb{E}_{\ensuremath{Q}_M}[f(\mathbf{x}')]} = c K.
    \end{equation}
